analysis.one_liner: Directs the Energy Department to help states and industry cut methane from oil and gas flaring and venting.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either House committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Department of Energy to run a program to reduce methane emissions from flaring and venting of natural gas during oil and gas production. It would not impose new federal rules; instead, it would give technical help to state officials and industry, speed up methane-capture technology, keep a database of state regulations, and send Congress a report with recommendations. The bill states that states remain the primary regulators of oil and gas production on state and private lands.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities near oil and gas operations and everyone exposed to methane, a potent greenhouse gas, would benefit if flaring and venting decline. The bill would also help oil and gas producers by developing cheaper ways to capture natural gas that is currently burned or released, turning waste into a saleable product.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People near oil and gas fields

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Energy to carry out a comprehensive program to reduce methane emissions from flaring and venting during oil and gas production.
Would provide technical assistance to state and local officials, Tribes, and industry, and accelerate development of technologies and practices that reduce flaring and venting.
Would maintain a database of each oil and gas producing state's flaring and venting rules and inform states of options to economically capture and use natural gas that would otherwise be wasted.
Would require a report to Congress on flaring and venting policies, technology barriers, and recommendations to reduce those barriers, with input from a public technical conference.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the Energy Department's program, and the oil and gas industry would be asked to participate and eventually adopt capture practices, though the bill imposes no mandates or penalties.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies entirely on voluntary technical assistance, databases, and reports; it sets no emission limits, standards, or deadlines, so methane from flaring and venting could continue largely unchanged.
It explicitly recognizes states as the primary regulators of production and emissions on state and private lands, which limits any federal backstop where state rules are weak.
An honest supporter would acknowledge that a bill with no cosponsors and no enforcement mechanism is unlikely to move methane levels on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to air quality and the climate is real but modest, because the bill offers no enforceable limits, only federal coordination, research, and advice. The cost to taxpayers is small. As a first step toward capturing wasted gas it is reasonable; as a response to methane emissions it is light-touch by design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Curtis introduced the Methane Emissions Reduction Act in the House on October 17, 2023, with no cosponsors.
On October 25, 2023, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in part, to the Science, Space, and Technology Committee.
On November 3, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials, and no further action was taken.
The bill received no hearing, markup, floor vote, or cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers are better off, since no federal program, report process, or expectations around flaring and venting were created. The public gained nothing, but also lost little, because the bill carried no enforceable requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers, by default

for.name: Rep. John Curtis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a federal technical-assistance program on methane flaring and venting.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 25, 2023, and never held a markup or advanced it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
against.what_they_did: Received part of the bill for consideration and took no action.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, was attached to the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill imposes no mandates or penalties on producers; instead it would offer federal technical assistance and help develop cheaper ways to capture gas now burned or vented, which producers can sell. Producers' interest in keeping state-level, voluntary regulation primary runs against stronger public emission rules, but the bill's actual mechanisms cost them nothing and could add revenue.
The bill would direct federal resources toward accelerating development and commercial use of flaring and venting reduction technologies, expanding this niche market.
